title: Every fast write moves work somewhere else
excerpt: A database write can stop after memory, a local SSD, an object PUT, or a replicated WAL. Each choice changes latency, durability, and who owns the work left for later.
content_html:
Every storage engine has to decide what must finish before it tells a client that a write succeeded. The quickest answer is to return after copying the bytes into memory. A local durable write waits for fdatasync() on an SSD in the database host. Keeping the write after that host disappears means waiting for a network volume, an object store, or several database servers to save their own copies.

Those choices move latency and durability together because returning after memory is fast, but a machine crash can lose the write. Waiting for a local SSD survives a process or kernel crash, but not the loss of that device or host, while remote storage or several database servers can survive more failures by putting network and copy time into every write.

One system’s fdatasync() waits for 1 SSD attached to the database host, while another exposes a network volume through the same NVMe interface and waits for a remote storage service. The syscall name is the same, but the latency and the failures the data survives are not.

Newer storage designs built around object storage make this choice especially interesting to me because many put immutable sorted files in object storage, use a host-local NVMe SSD for a write-ahead log or cache, and organize data with a log-structured merge tree (LSM) layout. Object storage can be a fantastic primitive to build around because the storage service can own the durable copies while compute comes and goes, and writing new immutable files avoids small random updates to shared disk pages.

After a successful object PUT, the storage service owns meeting its advertised durability for those bytes. The database still has to decide which version is current, record that decision so other machines can see it, make reads fast, remove old versions, and recover after a crash. A local write-ahead log can make writes faster, but then the database has to decide whether losing that local copy is acceptable or whether another copy must exist before success.

I use client PUT for the key-value request sent to the database, and object PUT for the HTTP request sent to object storage. Once I kept those writes separate, it became easier to follow 1 client PUT through memory, a local SSD, remote storage, and a durable majority of database servers. So when I see a very fast number for an operation, I want to know which operation pays for it, what can still be lost after success, and how much unfinished cleanup the system can tolerate.

I found it useful to start with the costs I would want from an append-only key-value store.

OperationWork before success
GETO(key bytes + returned bytes), 1 index lookup and 1 read for the value
PUTO(key bytes + payload bytes), 1 pass over the payload to hash it, 1 WAL append, and 1 fdatasync() shared with other writes
DELETEO(key bytes), append 1 delete record

These costs look attractive because a normal request never scans every retained object or walks the full write history, and a larger value costs more than a smaller value in an unsurprising way.

Those small request costs are possible because an index already maps each key to its latest value for GET, several PUT requests can share a device flush, and DELETE records that a value is dead without removing the old bytes immediately. The PUT is the easiest place to see where that work moves, so I started there.

How a client PUT reaches a local SSD

Here I mean a host-local NVMe SSD, which is attached to the same host as the database rather than reached through a remote storage service. Once a write is synced, it can survive a process or kernel crash, but losing the SSD or the host can still lose the write.

NVMe names the interface used to send commands to a device, but it does not tell us where the storage lives or which failures the data survives. A remote block volume can also appear as an NVMe device, even though each write crosses a network and a storage service keeps the copies. An NVMe latency number is incomplete without its acknowledgment point. Did the timer stop after copying bytes into memory, after syncing 1 local SSD, or after a remote volume acknowledged the write?

A local WAL is tempting because the latency gap can be large. AWS describes S3 Express One Zone as having consistent single-digit millisecond read and write request latency and being up to 10x faster than S3 Standard, while Turso measured a 4 KB PUT at 6.4 ms on average and 7 ms at p99. A local fdatasync() measured at 1 ms would make the local path about 6x faster, while 0.1 ms would make it about 64x faster. A 50x difference can be a real benchmark result, but it is not a property of every NVMe device and object store, and the 2 paths still survive different failures.

The local write separates copying bytes into memory from making them durable. A write-ahead log, or WAL, is an ordered record of changes that the database can replay after a crash. In a buffered implementation, a client PUT travels through the kernel and device like this.

write() can return once the WAL bytes reach page cache, but this design returns success only after fdatasync() reaches the local SSD.

On Linux, write() usually copies bytes into page cache, then the kernel marks those pages dirty and writes them to the device later. A process exit does not discard page cache, although a kernel crash or machine loss can erase dirty pages that have not reached storage.

fdatasync() waits for file data and the metadata needed to retrieve it. fsync() also flushes the file’s other metadata. Creating or renaming a file may require syncing its directory because the file contents and the directory entry that names it are separate writes.

O_DIRECT and io_uring do not change this durability point. O_DIRECT can bypass page cache, and io_uring can submit I/O efficiently, but neither turns an unsynced write into durable data. The filesystem and device still have to complete the writes and flushes required before the API can say that the data survived a crash.

fdatasync() may finish just before the connection breaks, leaving the WAL committed while the client never receives success. The client can supply an operation ID with the PUT, then retry the same ID and bytes to receive the recorded result, while reusing that ID with different bytes fails. Faster hardware shortens this window, but it cannot remove the ambiguity.

1 flush can cover many writes

Calling fdatasync() after every small client PUT is the easiest version to reason about, but throughput is now limited by how many flushes the device can finish. A serialized 1 ms flush allows roughly 1,000 flushes per second even when the device can stream far more bytes.

The WAL writer can share an expensive flush by putting appended records into the current batch and closing it after a fixed number of bytes, writes, or time. It remembers the final byte in that batch, calls fdatasync() on the WAL file, then returns success to every writer covered by that saved position. A write appended after the batch closes waits for the next flush.

PUT A through PUT D share 1 fdatasync() and receive success together. PUT E arrived after the batch closed, so it waits for the next SSD flush.

Several requests now wait on the same real flush, so successful writes still survive the same failures while throughput improves. The earliest request waits longest, a flush error fails the entire batch, and a timed-out request may already have bytes in a batch that later reaches disk.

Sharing a flush also requires limits for bytes, writes, and time, along with a limit on the pending-write queue because a slow device can otherwise let waiting writes consume all available memory. Under load, a batch often fills naturally while the previous flush is running, so sleeping to collect more writes can add latency without helping throughput.

The device cost depends on the size of the writes after batching. Moving 1 GiB/s through 256 KiB device writes needs about 4,096 input/output operations per second, while the same byte rate through 16 KiB device writes needs about 65,536. The number of client requests does not tell us that cost by itself because the sizes of writes that reach the device determine the required IOPS.

Keeping a write beyond the database host

Returning after local fdatasync() removes the object request from the time the client waits, but it changes what success means. The newest durable WAL records now exist on 1 SSD in 1 database host. If that host disappears before those records are uploaded, a replacement can only recover the older remote copy.

The database is now stateful in a way an object-only writer was not. A scheduler cannot move it to any machine and assume all successful writes will be there. The system must keep the SSD available, accept a window of data loss, or create another durable copy before success.

A durable network volume can keep the copy outside the compute host, an object store can keep it independently of the writer, and a replicated WAL can keep a copy on other database servers. Each option puts different work back into the time the client waits.

A durable network volume can still look like an ordinary block device to the database, while the storage service keeps copies outside the database host. Its fdatasync() includes a network request and whatever copying the service completes before acknowledging the write, so it is different from syncing the local SSD in the earlier diagram. The volume can outlive the database process and its host, although its copies may still live within 1 failure domain.

Each storage option has a different point where success becomes safe to return, which makes an unlabeled latency chart hard to interpret.

Success waits forLatency includesThe acknowledged write survives
Copy into page cacheMemory copyProcess exit, but not a kernel crash or machine loss
fdatasync() to a local SSDSSD write and cache flushProcess and kernel crash, but not SSD or host loss
fdatasync() to a durable network volumeStorage network and copies made by the volume serviceDatabase host loss; further coverage depends on the volume service
Successful object PUTHTTP request and copies made by the object serviceWriter and database host loss; further coverage depends on the object service
Durable WAL append on 2 of 3 serversNetwork transfer and disk sync on 2 serversLoss of 1 server, but not permanent loss of 2 servers before repair

The same question comes up with object storage, where a service may keep copies on several machines in 1 failure domain or spread them across several failure domains. Both are remote object writes, but they do not survive the same outage, so the number of copies alone does not describe durability. Putting a local WAL in front adds another choice because the database can finish the object upload before success or leave it for later.

Leaving the upload for later means returning after local fdatasync(), which keeps the write path short and lets the database upload full WAL files once they are no longer receiving writes. Losing the local SSD or its host can then lose every acknowledged record after the last uploaded byte, so the age of the oldest record waiting for upload tells us how much recent data is at risk.

Finishing the object PUT before success closes that window, but now every write includes the remote request. Batching reduces the request count, although the first writes in each batch wait longer for the batch to fill.

Local success leaves the newest WAL records on the database host until the dotted upload completes. Requiring the object PUT before success closes that window and adds the remote request to write latency.

At 1,000 writes per second, 1 object per write produces 2,592,000,000 object PUT requests in a 30-day month. Batching 100 writes per object reduces that to 25,920,000, while the earliest write in each batch waits longer and a failed request resends more bytes. The storage bill, write latency, and number of bytes resent after a failure all change together.

Batching changes the request count, but it does not decide what happens when 2 writers try to update the same object. On S3, conditional writes handle that narrower race. If-None-Match: * creates an object only if its key is absent, while If-Match: <etag> updates an object only if its current version matches. The losing request fails its precondition, so a caller can update a single object only when the expected version is still current. This does not make several objects visible as a single change or revoke an old writer’s access to other keys.

When the object PUT fits the write-latency budget, the database can stop here and let the storage service own the durable copies and decide which conditional update wins. When it does not fit, but every successful write still has to survive loss of the database host, the database can replicate its WAL across several hosts and wait for enough of them to sync it.

Replicating the WAL adds coordination

The replicated WAL turns 1 stateful database host into 3. A client sends its PUT to the leader, which appends the WAL entry locally and sends the same entry to 2 followers. Success can return after the leader and either follower have synced it, so the write survives loss of 1 server. Compared with 1 local SSD, every commit now includes a network trip and a second device sync.

Replicas placed close together can produce that durable majority faster than a general object request, while replicas spread across failure domains survive a larger outage and add more network time to the write. Copying the bytes is only part of the problem because the servers also have to decide who may write and which writes have committed.

The storage engine does not automatically need to run its own leader election because the data is important. Another service can assign a writer and give it a higher writer number, then storage can reject writes carrying an older number. Coordination still exists in that design, but it lives outside the storage engine. The replicas also need a rule for how many durable acknowledgments make a write committed. Consensus enters the storage engine when those servers must choose the writer and preserve 1 committed log themselves, including when some of them cannot communicate with the others.

In Raft, the leader records its current term, a number that increases after an election, and the write’s position in the log. It sends the write to the other servers, called followers, and commits it after a majority has saved the log through that position on disk.

The leader and the first follower to finish create 2 durable WAL copies before success. The other follower may finish later.

The disk and network operations can overlap, so healthy latency is close to the slower of the 2 operations that must finish rather than the sum of every disk write. Slow writes now include network delays and the time taken by the slower server needed for a majority. When the servers split into groups that cannot communicate, the group without a majority stops accepting writes because it cannot know whether the other group has a newer history.

A shortcut that often comes up is letting a follower acknowledge from RAM. The Raft paper instead writes the current term, vote, and log to disk before returning the related acknowledgment. The RAM acknowledgment is faster and survives fewer failures because those copies can disappear if the machines restart together or lose power, even though the client already saw success.

Replicating the write also leaves the system responsible for electing leaders, repairing different logs after a failure, copying missing writes to a server that fell behind, saving full copies for faster restart, adding and removing servers safely, and monitoring replication delay. None of that work appears in the latency of a single healthy write.

Fast reads require an index and cleanup

Being able to replay the WAL after a crash does not make GET cheap. Scanning the WAL for every read would make its cost grow with history, so the engine keeps a separate lookup from each key to its latest value or disk location.

O(key bytes + returned bytes) assumes the engine already knows where the current value lives. A hash index can give us that lookup without keeping keys in order. A B-tree supports ordered reads and range scans, while adding work that grows with the height of the tree and requiring page updates and occasional splits. An LSM writes recent keys into memory and sorted files, then merges and rewrites those files later.

An LSM and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) describe different parts of a database and can exist together. The LSM controls how keys move through memory and sorted files, while MVCC controls which versions readers and writers can see. An LSM later merges sorted files, an append-only blob store copies live values out of files containing dead bytes, and a page-based MVCC engine cleans up row versions that are no longer visible. Each algorithm leaves old bytes behind after a logical delete or replacement.

An O(key bytes) delete can append a delete record and update the lookup, while freeing the old value may later require reading the file index, copying values that are still current, switching reads to replacement files, and deleting files that no reader still uses.

Big O shows growth, not durability latency

Coming back to the original costs, the same client PUT remains O(key bytes + payload bytes) whether it stops at a local SSD, an object service, or a majority of database servers. Big O tells us how work grows as the key or value gets larger, but it does not show the difference between a device flush, a remote HTTP request, and a network round trip followed by 2 device flushes.

The growth term stays the same across these 3 paths, while the work before success changes.

Request pathWork that grows with the requestWork before success that Big O hides
PUT to a local WALO(key bytes + payload bytes)1 WAL append and a share of 1 local fdatasync()
PUT to object storageO(key bytes + payload bytes)Network round trip and object-service acknowledgment, shared across writes when batched
PUT to a replicated WALO(key bytes + payload bytes)Network transfer and durable WAL append on a majority

For GET and DELETE, the bounds rule out listing every object during a normal read, replaying the full WAL to find a key, or scanning all stored data to delete 1 value. They still do not say whether the fixed work takes microseconds or milliseconds, so a latency result needs the success point and percentile beside it.

The work left for later needs limits too, so a WAL file has a maximum size even though uploading it is O(file bytes). Cleanup may eventually inspect or rewrite the whole dataset, but each run needs a byte limit and a saved position so it can resume after a crash. The pending queue also needs a limit because writes can create old bytes faster than cleanup removes them, and without one the cheap request path only hides a queue that keeps growing.

LLMs make it much faster to write the uploader, cleanup loop, or replicated log without deciding how much unfinished work the system may keep or when it must slow writes down. They also cannot choose when success is safe to return, what a timeout means, or which crash may lose data. Those decisions still have to be written down and tested around fdatasync(), making an object current, replacing a writer, and copying a write to a majority of servers.

Following the write from memory to a local SSD, remote storage, and replicas made the tradeoff easier for me to reason about. The faster path usually stops after less work and survives fewer failures, while moving success later can buy more durability and may also make the database responsible for coordination, repair, and cleanup. The GET, PUT, and DELETE numbers only become useful once those choices are written beside them.

On S3, conditional writes handle that narrower race. If-None-Match: * creates an object only if its key is absent, while If-Match: updates an object only if its current version matches. The losing request fails its precondition, so a caller can update a single object only when the expected version is still current. This does not make several objects visible as a single change or revoke an old writer’s access to other keys.When the object PUT fits the write-latency budget, the database can stop here and let the storage service own the durable copies and decide which conditional update wins. When it does not fit, but every successful write still has to survive loss of the database host, the database can replicate its WAL across several hosts and wait for enough of them to sync it.Replicating the WAL adds coordinationThe replicated WAL turns 1 stateful database host into 3. A client sends its PUT to the leader, which appends the WAL entry locally and sends the same entry to 2 followers. Success can return after the leader and either follower have synced it, so the write survives loss of 1 server. Compared with 1 local SSD, every commit now includes a network trip and a second device sync.Replicas placed close together can produce that durable majority faster than a general object request, while replicas spread across failure domains survive a larger outage and add more network time to the write. Copying the bytes is only part of the problem because the servers also have to decide who may write and which writes have committed.The storage engine does not automatically need to run its own leader election because the data is important. Another service can assign a writer and give it a higher writer number, then storage can reject writes carrying an older number. Coordination still exists in that design, but it lives outside the storage engine. The replicas also need a rule for how many durable acknowledgments make a write committed. Consensus enters the storage engine when those servers must choose the writer and preserve 1 committed log themselves, including when some of them cannot communicate with the others.In Raft, the leader records its current term, a number that increases after an election, and the write’s position in the log. It sends the write to the other servers, called followers, and commits it after a majority has saved the log through that position on disk.--- config: look: handDrawn handDrawnSeed: 17 fontFamily: "SFMono-Regular, Consolas, monospace" flowchart: curve: linear --- flowchart TB C["client PUT"] --> L subgraph R["3-NODE REPLICATED WAL"] L["leader

The other follower may finish later.The disk and network operations can overlap, so healthy latency is close to the slower of the 2 operations that must finish rather than the sum of every disk write. Slow writes now include network delays and the time taken by the slower server needed for a majority. When the servers split into groups that cannot communicate, the group without a majority stops accepting writes because it cannot know whether the other group has a newer history.A shortcut that often comes up is letting a follower acknowledge from RAM. The Raft paper instead writes the current term, vote, and log to disk before returning the related acknowledgment. The RAM acknowledgment is faster and survives fewer failures because those copies can disappear if the machines restart together or lose power, even though the client already saw success.Replicating the write also leaves the system responsible for electing leaders, repairing different logs after a failure, copying missing writes to a server that fell behind, saving full copies for faster restart, adding and removing servers safely, and monitoring replication delay. None of that work appears in the latency of a single healthy write.Fast reads require an index and cleanupBeing able to replay the WAL after a crash does not make GET cheap. Scanning the WAL for every read would make its cost grow with history, so the engine keeps a separate lookup from each key to its latest value or disk location.O(key bytes + returned bytes) assumes the engine already knows where the current value lives. A hash index can give us that lookup without keeping keys in order. A B-tree supports ordered reads and range scans, while adding work that grows with the height of the tree and requiring page updates and occasional splits. An LSM writes recent keys into memory and sorted files, then merges and rewrites those files later.An LSM and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) describe different parts of a database and can exist together. The LSM controls how keys move through memory and sorted files, while MVCC controls which versions readers and writers can see. An LSM later merges sorted files, an append-only blob store copies live values out of files containing dead bytes, and a page-based MVCC engine cleans up row versions that are no longer visible. Each algorithm leaves old bytes behind after a logical delete or replacement.An O(key bytes) delete can append a delete record and update the lookup, while freeing the old value may later require reading the file index, copying values that are still current, switching reads to replacement files, and deleting files that no reader still uses.Big O shows growth, not durability latencyComing back to the original costs, the same client PUT remains O(key bytes + payload bytes) whether it stops at a local SSD, an object service, or a majority of database servers. Big O tells us how work grows as the key or value gets larger, but it does not show the difference between a device flush, a remote HTTP request, and a network round trip followed by 2 device flushes.The growth term stays the same across these 3 paths, while the work before success changes.Request pathWork that grows with the requestWork before success that Big O hidesPUT to a local WALO(key bytes + payload bytes)1 WAL append and a share of 1 local fdatasync()PUT to object storageO(key bytes + payload bytes)Network round trip and object-service acknowledgment, shared across writes when batchedPUT to a replicated WALO(key bytes + payload bytes)Network transfer and durable WAL append on a majorityFor GET and DELETE, the bounds rule out listing every object during a normal read, replaying the full WAL to find a key, or scanning all stored data to delete 1 value. They still do not say whether the fixed work takes microseconds or milliseconds, so a latency result needs the success point and percentile beside it.The work left for later needs limits too, so a WAL file has a maximum size even though uploading it is O(file bytes). Cleanup may eventually inspect or rewrite the whole dataset, but each run needs a byte limit and a saved position so it can resume after a crash. The pending queue also needs a limit because writes can create old bytes faster than cleanup removes them, and without one the cheap request path only hides a queue that keeps growing.LLMs make it much faster to write the uploader, cleanup loop, or replicated log without deciding how much unfinished work the system may keep or when it must slow writes down. They also cannot choose when success is safe to return, what a timeout means, or which crash may lose data. Those decisions still have to be written down and tested around fdatasync(), making an object current, replacing a writer, and copying a write to a majority of servers.Following the write from memory to a local SSD, remote storage, and replicas made the tradeoff easier for me to reason about. The faster path usually stops after less work and survives fewer failures, while moving success later can buy more durability and may also make the database responsible for coordination, repair, and cleanup. The GET, PUT, and DELETE numbers only become useful once those choices are written beside them.

blocks.html_en: Every storage engine has to decide what must finish before it tells a client that a write succeeded. The quickest answer is to return after copying the bytes into memory. A local durable write waits for fdatasync() on an SSD in the database host. Keeping the write after that host disappears means waiting for a network volume, an object store, or several database servers to save their own copies.

sentences.en: Every storage engine has to decide what must finish before it tells a client that a write succeeded.
sentences.zh: 每个存储引擎都必须决定在告诉客户端写入成功之前必须完成什么操作。

sentences.en: The quickest answer is to return after copying the bytes into memory.
sentences.zh: 最快的答案是将字节复制到内存后返回。

sentences.en: A local durable write waits for fdatasync() on an SSD in the database host.
sentences.zh: 本地持久写入等待数据库主机中 SSD 上的 fdatasync()。

sentences.en: Keeping the write after that host disappears means waiting for a network volume, an object store, or several database servers to save their own copies.
sentences.zh: 在该主机消失后保留写入意味着等待网络卷、对象存储或多个数据库服务器保存自己的副本。

blocks.html_en: Those choices move latency and durability together because returning after memory is fast, but a machine crash can lose the write. Waiting for a local SSD survives a process or kernel crash, but not the loss of that device or host, while remote storage or several database servers can survive more failures by putting network and copy time into every write.

sentences.en: Those choices move latency and durability together because returning after memory is fast, but a machine crash can lose the write.
sentences.zh: 这些选择将延迟和持久性结合在一起，因为内存返回速度很快，但机器崩溃可能会丢失写入。

sentences.en: Waiting for a local SSD survives a process or kernel crash, but not the loss of that device or host, while remote storage or several database servers can survive more failures by putting network and copy time into every write.
sentences.zh: 等待本地SSD可以在进程或内核崩溃时幸存下来，但不能在设备或主机丢失时幸存下来，而远程存储或多个数据库服务器可以通过将网络和复制时间放入每次写入中来幸存更多故障。

blocks.html_en: One system’s fdatasync() waits for 1 SSD attached to the database host, while another exposes a network volume through the same NVMe interface and waits for a remote storage service. The syscall name is the same, but the latency and the failures the data survives are not.

sentences.en: The syscall name is the same, but the latency and the failures the data survives are not.
sentences.zh: 系统调用名称相同，但数据存活的延迟和故障却不同。

blocks.html_en: Newer storage designs built around object storage make this choice especially interesting to me because many put immutable sorted files in object storage, use a host-local NVMe SSD for a write-ahead log or cache, and organize data with a log-structured merge tree (LSM) layout. Object storage can be a fantastic primitive to build around because the storage service can own the durable copies while compute comes and goes, and writing new immutable files avoids small random updates to shared disk pages.

sentences.en: Newer storage designs built around object storage make this choice especially interesting to me because many put immutable sorted files in object storage, use a host-local NVMe SSD for a write-ahead log or cache, and organize data with a log-structured merge tree (LSM) layout.
sentences.zh: 围绕对象存储构建的较新的存储设计使我对这种选择特别感兴趣，因为许多人将不可变的排序文件放入对象存储中，使用主机本地 NVMe SSD 进行预写日志或缓存，并使用日志结构合并树 (LSM) 布局组织数据。

sentences.en: Object storage can be a fantastic primitive to build around because the storage service can own the durable copies while compute comes and goes, and writing new immutable files avoids small random updates to shared disk pages.
sentences.zh: 对象存储可能是一个很棒的基础，因为存储服务可以在计算来来去去时拥有持久副本，并且编写新的不可变文件可以避免对共享磁盘页面进行小的随机更新。

blocks.html_en: After a successful object PUT, the storage service owns meeting its advertised durability for those bytes. The database still has to decide which version is current, record that decision so other machines can see it, make reads fast, remove old versions, and recover after a crash. A local write-ahead log can make writes faster, but then the database has to decide whether losing that local copy is acceptable or whether another copy must exist before success.

sentences.zh: 本地预写日志可以使写入速度更快，但数据库必须决定是否可以接受丢失本地副本，或者在成功之前是否必须存在另一个副本。

blocks.html_en: A local WAL is tempting because the latency gap can be large. AWS describes S3 Express One Zone as having consistent single-digit millisecond read and write request latency and being up to 10x faster than S3 Standard, while Turso measured a 4 KB PUT at 6.4 ms on average and 7 ms at p99. A local fdatasync() measured at 1 ms would make the local path about 6x faster, while 0.1 ms would make it about 64x faster. A 50x difference can be a real benchmark result, but it is not a property of every NVMe device and object store, and the 2 paths still survive different failures.

blocks.html_en: Calling fdatasync() after every small client PUT is the easiest version to reason about, but throughput is now limited by how many flushes the device can finish. A serialized 1 ms flush allows roughly 1,000 flushes per second even when the device can stream far more bytes.

sentences.en: Calling fdatasync() after every small client PUT is the easiest version to reason about, but throughput is now limited by how many flushes the device can finish.
sentences.zh: 在每个小客户端 PUT 之后调用 fdatasync() 是最容易推理的版本，但吞吐量现在受到设备可以完成的刷新次数的限制。

sentences.en: A serialized 1 ms flush allows roughly 1,000 flushes per second even when the device can stream far more bytes.
sentences.zh: 即使设备可以传输更多字节，串行化的 1 毫秒刷新也允许每秒大约 1,000 次刷新。

blocks.html_en: The WAL writer can share an expensive flush by putting appended records into the current batch and closing it after a fixed number of bytes, writes, or time. It remembers the final byte in that batch, calls fdatasync() on the WAL file, then returns success to every writer covered by that saved position. A write appended after the batch closes waits for the next flush.

sentences.en: The WAL writer can share an expensive flush by putting appended records into the current batch and closing it after a fixed number of bytes, writes, or time.
sentences.zh: WAL 写入器可以通过将附加记录放入当前批次并在固定数量的字节、写入或时间后关闭它来共享昂贵的刷新。

sentences.en: It remembers the final byte in that batch, calls fdatasync() on the WAL file, then returns success to every writer covered by that saved position.
sentences.zh: 它会记住该批次中的最后一个字节，对 WAL 文件调用 fdatasync()，然后将成功返回给该保存位置覆盖的每个写入器。

sentences.en: A write appended after the batch closes waits for the next flush.
sentences.zh: 批处理关闭后追加的写入等待下一次刷新。

blocks.html_en: PUT A through PUT D share 1 fdatasync() and receive success together. PUT E arrived after the batch closed, so it waits for the next SSD flush.

sentences.en: PUT A through PUT D share 1 fdatasync() and receive success together.
sentences.zh: PUT A 到 PUT D 共享 1 个 fdatasync() 并一起接收成功。

sentences.en: PUT E arrived after the batch closed, so it waits for the next SSD flush.
sentences.zh: PUT E 在批次关闭后到达，因此它等待下一次 SSD 刷新。

blocks.html_en: Several requests now wait on the same real flush, so successful writes still survive the same failures while throughput improves. The earliest request waits longest, a flush error fails the entire batch, and a timed-out request may already have bytes in a batch that later reaches disk.

sentences.en: Several requests now wait on the same real flush, so successful writes still survive the same failures while throughput improves.
sentences.zh: 现在，多个请求等待相同的实际刷新，因此成功的写入仍然可以在相同的失败中幸存下来，同时吞吐量提高。

sentences.en: The earliest request waits longest, a flush error fails the entire batch, and a timed-out request may already have bytes in a batch that later reaches disk.
sentences.zh: 最早的请求等待时间最长，刷新错误会导致整个批次失败，并且超时的请求可能已经有批次中的字节稍后到达磁盘。

blocks.html_en: Sharing a flush also requires limits for bytes, writes, and time, along with a limit on the pending-write queue because a slow device can otherwise let waiting writes consume all available memory. Under load, a batch often fills naturally while the previous flush is running, so sleeping to collect more writes can add latency without helping throughput.

sentences.en: Sharing a flush also requires limits for bytes, writes, and time, along with a limit on the pending-write queue because a slow device can otherwise let waiting writes consume all available memory.
sentences.zh: 共享刷新还需要限制字节、写入和时间，以及对挂起写入队列的限制，因为慢速设备可能会让等待写入消耗所有可用内存。

sentences.en: Under load, a batch often fills naturally while the previous flush is running, so sleeping to collect more writes can add latency without helping throughput.
sentences.zh: 在负载下，当上一个刷新正在运行时，批次通常会自然填充，因此休眠以收集更多写入会增加延迟，而不会提高吞吐量。

blocks.html_en: The device cost depends on the size of the writes after batching. Moving 1 GiB/s through 256 KiB device writes needs about 4,096 input/output operations per second, while the same byte rate through 16 KiB device writes needs about 65,536. The number of client requests does not tell us that cost by itself because the sizes of writes that reach the device determine the required IOPS.

sentences.en: The device cost depends on the size of the writes after batching.
sentences.zh: 设备成本取决于批处理后写入的大小。

sentences.en: Moving 1 GiB/s through 256 KiB device writes needs about 4,096 input/output operations per second, while the same byte rate through 16 KiB device writes needs about 65,536.
sentences.zh: 通过 256 KiB 设备写入移动 1 GiB/s 每秒大约需要 4,096 次输入/输出操作，而通过 16 KiB 设备写入相同的字节率大约需要 65,536 次。

sentences.en: The number of client requests does not tell us that cost by itself because the sizes of writes that reach the device determine the required IOPS.
sentences.zh: 客户端请求的数量本身并不能告诉我们成本，因为到达设备的写入大小决定了所需的 IOPS。

blocks.html_en: Returning after local fdatasync() removes the object request from the time the client waits, but it changes what success means. The newest durable WAL records now exist on 1 SSD in 1 database host. If that host disappears before those records are uploaded, a replacement can only recover the older remote copy.

sentences.en: Returning after local fdatasync() removes the object request from the time the client waits, but it changes what success means.
sentences.zh: 在本地 fdatasync() 之后返回会从客户端等待的时间中删除对象请求，但它改变了成功的含义。

sentences.en: The newest durable WAL records now exist on 1 SSD in 1 database host.
sentences.zh: 最新的持久 WAL 记录现在存在于 1 台数据库主机的 1 个 SSD 上。

sentences.en: If that host disappears before those records are uploaded, a replacement can only recover the older remote copy.
sentences.zh: 如果该主机在上传这些记录之前消失，则替换主机只能恢复较旧的远程副本。

blocks.html_en: The database is now stateful in a way an object-only writer was not. A scheduler cannot move it to any machine and assume all successful writes will be there. The system must keep the SSD available, accept a window of data loss, or create another durable copy before success.

sentences.en: The database is now stateful in a way an object-only writer was not.
sentences.zh: 数据库现在是有状态的，而纯对象编写器则没有。

sentences.en: A scheduler cannot move it to any machine and assume all successful writes will be there.
sentences.zh: 调度程序无法将其移动到任何机器并假设所有成功的写入都将在那里。

sentences.en: The system must keep the SSD available, accept a window of data loss, or create another durable copy before success.
sentences.zh: 系统必须保持 SSD 可用、接受数据丢失窗口或在成功之前创建另一个持久副本。

blocks.html_en: A durable network volume can keep the copy outside the compute host, an object store can keep it independently of the writer, and a replicated WAL can keep a copy on other database servers. Each option puts different work back into the time the client waits.

sentences.en: A durable network volume can keep the copy outside the compute host, an object store can keep it independently of the writer, and a replicated WAL can keep a copy on other database servers.
sentences.zh: 持久网络卷可以将副本保存在计算主机之外，对象存储可以将其独立于编写器，而复制的 WAL 可以在其他数据库服务器上保存副本。

sentences.en: Each option puts different work back into the time the client waits.
sentences.zh: 每个选项都会在客户等待的时间中投入不同的工作。

blocks.html_en: A durable network volume can still look like an ordinary block device to the database, while the storage service keeps copies outside the database host. Its fdatasync() includes a network request and whatever copying the service completes before acknowledging the write, so it is different from syncing the local SSD in the earlier diagram. The volume can outlive the database process and its host, although its copies may still live within 1 failure domain.

sentences.en: A durable network volume can still look like an ordinary block device to the database, while the storage service keeps copies outside the database host.
sentences.zh: 对于数据库来说，持久网络卷仍然看起来像普通的块设备，而存储服务将副本保留在数据库主机外部。

sentences.en: Its fdatasync() includes a network request and whatever copying the service completes before acknowledging the write, so it is different from syncing the local SSD in the earlier diagram.
sentences.zh: 它的 fdatasync() 包括网络请求以及在确认写入之前完成的任何复制服务，因此它与前面图中同步本地 SSD 不同。

sentences.en: The volume can outlive the database process and its host, although its copies may still live within 1 failure domain.
sentences.zh: 尽管卷的副本可能仍存在于 1 个故障域内，但该卷的寿命可能比数据库进程及其主机的寿命长。

blocks.html_en: Each storage option has a different point where success becomes safe to return, which makes an unlabeled latency chart hard to interpret.

sentences.en: Each storage option has a different point where success becomes safe to return, which makes an unlabeled latency chart hard to interpret.
sentences.zh: 每个存储选项都有一个不同的点，在该点上成功可以安全返回，这使得未标记的延迟图表难以解释。

blocks.html_en: The same question comes up with object storage, where a service may keep copies on several machines in 1 failure domain or spread them across several failure domains. Both are remote object writes, but they do not survive the same outage, so the number of copies alone does not describe durability. Putting a local WAL in front adds another choice because the database can finish the object upload before success or leave it for later.

sentences.en: The same question comes up with object storage, where a service may keep copies on several machines in 1 failure domain or spread them across several failure domains.
sentences.zh: 同样的问题也出现在对象存储中，其中服务可能会在 1 个故障域中的多台计算机上保存副本，或者将它们分布在多个故障域中。

sentences.en: Both are remote object writes, but they do not survive the same outage, so the number of copies alone does not describe durability.
sentences.zh: 两者都是远程对象写入，但它们无法在相同的中断中幸存，因此副本数量本身并不能描述持久性。

sentences.en: Putting a local WAL in front adds another choice because the database can finish the object upload before success or leave it for later.
sentences.zh: 将本地 WAL 放在前面增加了另一种选择，因为数据库可以在成功之前完成对象上传，也可以稍后再完成。

blocks.html_en: Leaving the upload for later means returning after local fdatasync(), which keeps the write path short and lets the database upload full WAL files once they are no longer receiving writes. Losing the local SSD or its host can then lose every acknowledged record after the last uploaded byte, so the age of the oldest record waiting for upload tells us how much recent data is at risk.

sentences.en: Leaving the upload for later means returning after local fdatasync(), which keeps the write path short and lets the database upload full WAL files once they are no longer receiving writes.
sentences.zh: 稍后上传意味着在本地 fdatasync() 之后返回，这会保持写入路径较短，并让数据库在不再接收写入时上传完整的 WAL 文件。

sentences.en: Losing the local SSD or its host can then lose every acknowledged record after the last uploaded byte, so the age of the oldest record waiting for upload tells us how much recent data is at risk.
sentences.zh: 丢失本地 SSD 或其主机可能会丢失最后上传字节后的每条已确认记录，因此等待上传的最旧记录的年龄告诉我们有多少最新数据面临风险。

blocks.html_en: Finishing the object PUT before success closes that window, but now every write includes the remote request. Batching reduces the request count, although the first writes in each batch wait longer for the batch to fill.

sentences.en: Finishing the object PUT before success closes that window, but now every write includes the remote request.
sentences.zh: 在成功之前完成对象 PUT 会关闭该窗口，但现在每次写入都包含远程请求。

sentences.en: Batching reduces the request count, although the first writes in each batch wait longer for the batch to fill.
sentences.zh: 批处理减少了请求计数，尽管每个批次中的第一次写入等待批次填充的时间更长。

blocks.html_en: Local success leaves the newest WAL records on the database host until the dotted upload completes. Requiring the object PUT before success closes that window and adds the remote request to write latency.

sentences.en: Local success leaves the newest WAL records on the database host until the dotted upload completes.
sentences.zh: 本地成功会将最新的 WAL 记录保留在数据库主机上，直到点上传完成。

sentences.en: Requiring the object PUT before success closes that window and adds the remote request to write latency.
sentences.zh: 在成功之前要求对象 PUT 会关闭该窗口并添加远程请求写入延迟。

blocks.html_en: At 1,000 writes per second, 1 object per write produces 2,592,000,000 object PUT requests in a 30-day month. Batching 100 writes per object reduces that to 25,920,000, while the earliest write in each batch waits longer and a failed request resends more bytes. The storage bill, write latency, and number of bytes resent after a failure all change together.

sentences.en: At 1,000 writes per second, 1 object per write produces 2,592,000,000 object PUT requests in a 30-day month.
sentences.zh: 如果每秒写入 1,000 次，则每次写入 1 个对象会在一个月 30 天的时间内产生 2,592,000,000 个对象 PUT 请求。

sentences.en: Batching 100 writes per object reduces that to 25,920,000, while the earliest write in each batch waits longer and a failed request resends more bytes.
sentences.zh: 每个对象批量写入 100 次可将写入量减少到 25,920,000，而每批中最早的写入会等待更长的时间，并且失败的请求会重新发送更多字节。

sentences.en: The storage bill, write latency, and number of bytes resent after a failure all change together.
sentences.zh: 存储费用、写入延迟和故障后重新发送的字节数都会一起发生变化。

blocks.html_en: Batching changes the request count, but it does not decide what happens when 2 writers try to update the same object. On S3, conditional writes handle that narrower race. If-None-Match: * creates an object only if its key is absent, while If-Match: <etag> updates an object only if its current version matches. The losing request fails its precondition, so a caller can update a single object only when the expected version is still current. This does not make several objects visible as a single change or revoke an old writer’s access to other keys.

sentences.en: Batching changes the request count, but it does not decide what happens when 2 writers try to update the same object.
sentences.zh: 批处理会更改请求计数，但它不会决定当 2 个写入者尝试更新同一对象时会发生什么。

sentences.en: On S3, conditional writes handle that narrower race.
sentences.zh: 在 S3 上，条件写入处理较小的竞争。

sentences.en: If-None-Match: * creates an object only if its key is absent, while If-Match: <etag> updates an object only if its current version matches.
sentences.zh: If-None-Match: * 仅当对象的键不存在时才创建对象，而 If-Match: <etag> 仅当其当前版本匹配时才更新对象。

sentences.en: The losing request fails its precondition, so a caller can update a single object only when the expected version is still current.
sentences.zh: 失败的请求未满足其先决条件，因此调用者仅当预期版本仍然是最新时才能更新单个对象。

sentences.en: This does not make several objects visible as a single change or revoke an old writer’s access to other keys.
sentences.zh: 这不会使多个对象作为单个更改可见，也不会撤销旧编写者对其他键的访问权限。

blocks.html_en: When the object PUT fits the write-latency budget, the database can stop here and let the storage service own the durable copies and decide which conditional update wins. When it does not fit, but every successful write still has to survive loss of the database host, the database can replicate its WAL across several hosts and wait for enough of them to sync it.

sentences.en: When the object PUT fits the write-latency budget, the database can stop here and let the storage service own the durable copies and decide which conditional update wins.
sentences.zh: 当对象 PUT 符合写入延迟预算时，数据库可以在此停止并让存储服务拥有持久副本并决定哪个条件更新获胜。

sentences.en: When it does not fit, but every successful write still has to survive loss of the database host, the database can replicate its WAL across several hosts and wait for enough of them to sync it.
sentences.zh: 当它不适合时，但每个成功的写入仍然必须在数据库主机丢失的情况下幸存下来，数据库可以在多个主机上复制其 WAL 并等待足够多的主机来同步它。

blocks.html_en: Replicating the WAL adds coordination

sentences.en: Replicating the WAL adds coordination
sentences.zh: 复制 WAL 增加协调

blocks.html_en: The replicated WAL turns 1 stateful database host into 3. A client sends its PUT to the leader, which appends the WAL entry locally and sends the same entry to 2 followers. Success can return after the leader and either follower have synced it, so the write survives loss of 1 server. Compared with 1 local SSD, every commit now includes a network trip and a second device sync.

sentences.en: The replicated WAL turns 1 stateful database host into 3.
sentences.zh: 复制的 WAL 将 1 个有状态数据库主机变成 3 个。

sentences.en: A client sends its PUT to the leader, which appends the WAL entry locally and sends the same entry to 2 followers.
sentences.zh: 客户端将其 PUT 发送给领导者，领导者在本地附加 WAL 条目并将相同的条目发送给 2 个追随者。

sentences.en: Success can return after the leader and either follower have synced it, so the write survives loss of 1 server.
sentences.zh: 在领导者和任一追随者同步后可以返回成功，因此写入不会丢失 1 个服务器。

sentences.en: Compared with 1 local SSD, every commit now includes a network trip and a second device sync.
sentences.zh: 与 1 个本地 SSD 相比，每次提交现在都包含一次网络行程和第二个设备同步。

blocks.html_en: Replicas placed close together can produce that durable majority faster than a general object request, while replicas spread across failure domains survive a larger outage and add more network time to the write. Copying the bytes is only part of the problem because the servers also have to decide who may write and which writes have committed.

sentences.en: Replicas placed close together can produce that durable majority faster than a general object request, while replicas spread across failure domains survive a larger outage and add more network time to the write.
sentences.zh: 靠近放置的副本可以比一般对象请求更快地产生持久多数，而分布在故障域中的副本可以承受更大的中断并增加更多的网络写入时间。

sentences.en: Copying the bytes is only part of the problem because the servers also have to decide who may write and which writes have committed.
sentences.zh: 复制字节只是问题的一部分，因为服务器还必须决定谁可以写入以及哪些写入已提交。

blocks.html_en: The storage engine does not automatically need to run its own leader election because the data is important. Another service can assign a writer and give it a higher writer number, then storage can reject writes carrying an older number. Coordination still exists in that design, but it lives outside the storage engine. The replicas also need a rule for how many durable acknowledgments make a write committed. Consensus enters the storage engine when those servers must choose the writer and preserve 1 committed log themselves, including when some of them cannot communicate with the others.

sentences.en: The storage engine does not automatically need to run its own leader election because the data is important.
sentences.zh: 存储引擎不会自动运行自己的领导者选举，因为数据很重要。

sentences.en: Another service can assign a writer and give it a higher writer number, then storage can reject writes carrying an older number.
sentences.zh: 另一个服务可以分配一个写入器并给它一个更高的写入器编号，然后存储可以拒绝携带旧编号的写入。

sentences.en: Coordination still exists in that design, but it lives outside the storage engine.
sentences.zh: 该设计中仍然存在协调，但它存在于存储引擎之外。

sentences.en: The replicas also need a rule for how many durable acknowledgments make a write committed.
sentences.zh: 副本还需要一个规则来确定有多少持久确认可以提交写入。

sentences.en: Consensus enters the storage engine when those servers must choose the writer and preserve 1 committed log themselves, including when some of them cannot communicate with the others.
sentences.zh: 当这些服务器必须选择写入者并自行保留 1 个已提交的日志时，包括其中一些服务器无法与其他服务器通信时，共识就会进入存储引擎。

blocks.html_en: In Raft, the leader records its current term, a number that increases after an election, and the write’s position in the log. It sends the write to the other servers, called followers, and commits it after a majority has saved the log through that position on disk.

sentences.en: In Raft, the leader records its current term, a number that increases after an election, and the write’s position in the log.
sentences.zh: 在 Raft 中，领导者记录其当前任期、选举后增加的数字以及写入在日志中的位置。

sentences.en: It sends the write to the other servers, called followers, and commits it after a majority has saved the log through that position on disk.

content_html_zh:
每个存储引擎都必须决定在告诉客户端写入成功之前必须完成什么操作。 最快的答案是将字节复制到内存后返回。 本地持久写入等待数据库主机中 SSD 上的 fdatasync()。 在该主机消失后保留写入意味着等待网络卷、对象存储或多个数据库服务器保存自己的副本。

这些选择将延迟和持久性结合在一起，因为内存返回速度很快，但机器崩溃可能会丢失写入。 等待本地SSD可以在进程或内核崩溃时幸存下来，但不能在设备或主机丢失时幸存下来，而远程存储或多个数据库服务器可以通过将网络和复制时间放入每次写入中来幸存更多故障。

一个系统的 fdatasync() 等待 1 个 SSD 连接到数据库主机，而另一个系统通过相同的 NVMe 接口公开网络卷并等待远程存储服务。 系统调用名称相同，但数据存活的延迟和故障却不同。

围绕对象存储构建的较新的存储设计使我对这种选择特别感兴趣，因为许多人将不可变的排序文件放入对象存储中，使用主机本地 NVMe SSD 进行预写日志或缓存，并使用日志结构合并树 (LSM) 布局组织数据。 对象存储可能是一个很棒的基础，因为存储服务可以在计算来来去去时拥有持久副本，并且编写新的不可变文件可以避免对共享磁盘页面进行小的随机更新。

成功进行对象 PUT 后，存储服务就拥有满足其所宣传的这些字节的持久性的要求。 数据库仍然必须决定哪个版本是当前版本，记录该决定，以便其他机器可以看到它，加快读取速度，删除旧版本，并在崩溃后恢复。 本地预写日志可以使写入速度更快，但数据库必须决定是否可以接受丢失本地副本，或者在成功之前是否必须存在另一个副本。

我使用客户端 PUT 来发送到数据库的键值请求，使用对象 PUT 来发送到对象存储的 HTTP 请求。 一旦我将这些写入分开，就可以更轻松地通过内存、本地 SSD、远程存储和大多数持久数据库服务器来跟踪 1 个客户端 PUT。 因此，当我看到某个操作的速度非常快时，我想知道哪个操作为此付出了代价，成功后仍然会丢失什么，以及系统可以容忍多少未完成的清理。

我发现从我想要从仅附加键值存储中获得的成本开始是很有用的。

手术先工作后成功
GETO（键字节 + 返回字节），1 次索引查找和 1 次读取值
PUTO（密钥字节 + 有效负载字节），1 次传递有效负载以对其进行哈希处理，1 次 WAL 附加，以及 1 次与其他写入共享的 fdatasync()
删除O(key bytes),追加1条删除记录

这些成本看起来很有吸引力，因为正常的请求不会扫描每个保留的对象或遍历完整的写入历史记录，并且毫不奇怪，较大的值比较小的值成本更高。

这些小的请求成本是可能的，因为索引已经将每个键映射到 GET 的最新值，多个 PUT 请求可以共享设备刷新，并且 DELETE 记录值已失效而无需立即删除旧字节。 PUT 是最容易看到工作进展的地方，所以我从那里开始。

客户端 PUT 如何到达本地 SSD

这里我指的是主机本地 NVMe SSD，它与数据库连接到同一主机，而不是通过远程存储服务访问。 一旦写入被同步，它就可以在进程或内核崩溃时幸存下来，但丢失 SSD 或主机仍然会丢失写入。

NVMe 命名了用于向设备发送命令的接口，但它并没有告诉我们存储位于何处或数据在哪些故障下仍然存在。 远程块卷也可以显示为 NVMe 设备，即使每次写入都跨网络并且存储服务保留副本。 如果没有确认点，NVMe 延迟数字是不完整的。 将字节复制到内存后、同步 1 个本地 SSD 后或远程卷确认写入后，计时器是否停止？

本地 WAL 很有吸引力，因为延迟差距可能很大。 AWS 将 S3 Express One Zone 描述为具有一致的个位数毫秒读取和写入请求延迟，比 S3 标准快 10 倍，而 Turso 测量的 4 KB PUT 平均为 6.4 毫秒，p99 为 7 毫秒。 以 1 毫秒测量的本地 fdatasync() 将使本地路径速度加快约 6 倍，而 0.1 毫秒则使其速度加快约 64 倍。 50 倍的差异可能是真正的基准测试结果，但这并不是每个 NVMe 设备和对象存储的属性，并且 2 条路径仍然可以承受不同的故障。

本地写入将字节复制到内存中与使它们持久化分开。 预写日志（WAL）是数据库可以在崩溃后重播的有序更改记录。 在缓冲实现中，客户端 PUT 像这样穿过内核和设备。

一旦 WAL 字节到达页缓存， write() 就可以返回，但此设计仅在 fdatasync() 到达本地 SSD 后才返回成功。

在 Linux 上，write() 通常将字节复制到页缓存中，然后内核将这些页标记为脏页，并稍后将它们写入设备。 尽管内核崩溃或机器丢失可以擦除尚未到达存储的脏页，但进程退出不会丢弃页缓存。

fdatasync() 等待文件数据和检索它所需的元数据。 fsync() 还会刷新文件的其他元数据。 创建或重命名文件可能需要同步其目录，因为文件内容和命名它的目录条目是单独写入的。

O_DIRECT 和 io_uring 不会更改此持久点。 O_DIRECT 可以绕过页面缓存，io_uring 可以有效地提交 I/O，但两者都不能将未同步的写入转化为持久数据。 文件系统和设备仍然必须完成所需的写入和刷新，然后 API 才能判断数据在崩溃中幸存下来。

fdatasync() 可能会在连接中断之前完成，导致 WAL 提交，而客户端永远不会收到成功。 客户端可以通过 PUT 提供操作 ID，然后重试相同的 ID 和字节以接收记录的结果，而以不同的字节重用该 ID 会失败。 更快的硬件会缩短这个窗口，但无法消除歧义。

1次刷新可以覆盖许多写入

在每个小客户端 PUT 之后调用 fdatasync() 是最容易推理的版本，但吞吐量现在受到设备可以完成的刷新次数的限制。 即使设备可以传输更多字节，串行化的 1 毫秒刷新也允许每秒大约 1,000 次刷新。

WAL 写入器可以通过将附加记录放入当前批次并在固定数量的字节、写入或时间后关闭它来共享昂贵的刷新。 它会记住该批次中的最后一个字节，对 WAL 文件调用 fdatasync()，然后将成功返回给该保存位置覆盖的每个写入器。 批处理关闭后追加的写入等待下一次刷新。

在数据库主机之外保持写入

在本地 fdatasync() 之后返回会从客户端等待的时间中删除对象请求，但它改变了成功的含义。 最新的持久 WAL 记录现在存在于 1 台数据库主机的 1 个 SSD 上。 如果该主机在上传这些记录之前消失，则替换主机只能恢复较旧的远程副本。

数据库现在是有状态的，而纯对象编写器则没有。 调度程序无法将其移动到任何机器并假设所有成功的写入都将在那里。 系统必须保持 SSD 可用、接受数据丢失窗口或在成功之前创建另一个持久副本。

持久网络卷可以将副本保存在计算主机之外，对象存储可以将其独立于编写器，而复制的 WAL 可以在其他数据库服务器上保存副本。 每个选项都会在客户等待的时间中投入不同的工作。

对于数据库来说，持久网络卷仍然看起来像普通的块设备，而存储服务将副本保留在数据库主机外部。 它的 fdatasync() 包括网络请求以及在确认写入之前完成的任何复制服务，因此它与前面图中同步本地 SSD 不同。 尽管卷的副本可能仍存在于 1 个故障域内，但该卷的寿命可能比数据库进程及其主机的寿命长。

每个存储选项都有一个不同的点，在该点上成功可以安全返回，这使得未标记的延迟图表难以解释。

同样的问题也出现在对象存储中，其中服务可能会在 1 个故障域中的多台计算机上保存副本，或者将它们分布在多个故障域中。 两者都是远程对象写入，但它们无法在相同的中断中幸存，因此副本数量本身并不能描述持久性。 将本地 WAL 放在前面增加了另一种选择，因为数据库可以在成功之前完成对象上传，也可以稍后再完成。

稍后上传意味着在本地 fdatasync() 之后返回，这会保持写入路径较短，并让数据库在不再接收写入时上传完整的 WAL 文件。 丢失本地 SSD 或其主机可能会丢失最后上传字节后的每条已确认记录，因此等待上传的最旧记录的年龄告诉我们有多少最新数据面临风险。

在成功之前完成对象 PUT 会关闭该窗口，但现在每次写入都包含远程请求。 批处理减少了请求计数，尽管每个批次中的第一次写入等待批次填充的时间更长。

如果每秒写入 1,000 次，则每次写入 1 个对象会在一个月 30 天的时间内产生 2,592,000,000 个对象 PUT 请求。 每个对象批量写入 100 次可将写入量减少到 25,920,000，而每批中最早的写入会等待更长的时间，并且失败的请求会重新发送更多字节。 存储费用、写入延迟和故障后重新发送的字节数都会一起发生变化。

批处理会更改请求计数，但它不会决定当 2 个写入者尝试更新同一对象时会发生什么。 在 S3 上，条件写入处理较小的竞争。 If-None-Match: * 仅当对象的键不存在时才创建对象，而 If-Match: <etag> 仅当其当前版本匹配时才更新对象。 失败的请求未满足其先决条件，因此调用者仅当预期版本仍然是最新时才能更新单个对象。 这不会使多个对象作为单个更改可见，也不会撤销旧编写者对其他键的访问权限。

当对象 PUT 符合写入延迟预算时，数据库可以在此停止并让存储服务拥有持久副本并决定哪个条件更新获胜。 当它不适合时，但每个成功的写入仍然必须在数据库主机丢失的情况下幸存下来，数据库可以在多个主机上复制其 WAL 并等待足够多的主机来同步它。

复制 WAL 增加协调

复制的 WAL 将 1 个有状态数据库主机变成 3 个。 客户端将其 PUT 发送给领导者，领导者在本地附加 WAL 条目并将相同的条目发送给 2 个追随者。 在领导者和任一追随者同步后可以返回成功，因此写入不会丢失 1 个服务器。 与 1 个本地 SSD 相比，每次提交现在都包含一次网络行程和第二个设备同步。

靠近放置的副本可以比一般对象请求更快地产生持久多数，而分布在故障域中的副本可以承受更大的中断并增加更多的网络写入时间。 复制字节只是问题的一部分，因为服务器还必须决定谁可以写入以及哪些写入已提交。

存储引擎不会自动运行自己的领导者选举，因为数据很重要。 另一个服务可以分配一个写入器并给它一个更高的写入器编号，然后存储可以拒绝携带旧编号的写入。 该设计中仍然存在协调，但它存在于存储引擎之外。 副本还需要一个规则来确定有多少持久确认可以提交写入。 当这些服务器必须选择写入者并自行保留 1 个已提交的日志时，包括其中一些服务器无法与其他服务器通信时，共识就会进入存储引擎。

在 Raft 中，领导者记录其当前任期、选举后增加的数字以及写入在日志中的位置。 它将写入发送到其他服务器（称为追随者），并在大多数服务器通过磁盘上的该位置保存日志后提交它。

磁盘和网络操作可以重叠，因此健康的延迟接近于必须完成的两个操作中较慢的一个，而不是每个磁盘写入的总和。 缓慢的写入现在包括网络延迟和大多数较慢的服务器所需的时间。 当服务器分成无法通信的组时，没有多数的组将停止接受写入，因为它无法知道另一个组是否有更新的历史记录。

经常出现的一个捷径是让关注者从 RAM 中进行确认。 Raft 论文在返回相关确认之前将当前术语、投票和日志写入磁盘。 RAM 确认速度更快，故障更少，因为如果机器一起重新启动或断电，这些副本可能会消失，即使客户端已经看到成功。

复制写入还让系统负责选举领导者、在故障后修复不同的日志、将丢失的写入复制到落后的服务器、保存完整副本以更快地重新启动、安全地添加和删除服务器以及监控复制延迟。 这些工作都不会出现在单个健康写入的延迟中。

快速读取需要索引和清理

崩溃后能够重放 WAL 并不会让 GET 变得便宜。 扫描 WAL 进行每次读取都会使其成本随着历史记录而增长，因此引擎会单独查找每个键到其最新值或磁盘位置。

O(key bytes + returned bytes) 假设引擎已经知道当前值所在的位置。 哈希索引可以为我们提供查找，而无需保持键的顺序。 B 树支持有序读取和范围扫描，同时添加随树高度增长的工作，并需要页面更新和偶尔的拆分。 LSM 将最近的键写入内存并排序文件，然后合并并重写这些文件。

LSM 和多版本并发控制 (MVCC) 描述数据库的不同部分，并且可以共存。 LSM 控制键如何在内存中移动和排序文件，而 MVCC 控制读取器和写入器可以看到哪些版本。 随后，LSM 会合并已排序的文件，仅附加 Blob 存储会从包含死字节的文件中复制实时值，基于页面的 MVCC 引擎会清理不再可见的行版本。 每个算法在逻辑删除或替换后都会留下旧字节。

O（键字节）删除可以附加删除记录并更新查找，而释放旧值可能稍后需要读取文件索引，复制仍然是当前的值，将读取切换到替换文件，以及删除没有读者仍在使用的文件。

大 O 显示增长，而不是持久性延迟

回到最初的成本，相同的客户端 PUT 仍然是 O（密钥字节 + 有效负载字节），无论它停止在本地 SSD、对象服务还是大多数数据库服务器上。 Big O 告诉我们工作如何随着键或值变大而增长，但它没有显示设备刷新、远程 HTTP 请求和随后进行 2 次设备刷新的网络往返之间的区别。

这 3 条路径的增长期限保持不变，但成功之前的工作发生了变化。

对于 GET 和 DELETE，界限排除了在正常读取期间列出每个对象、重播完整 WAL 以查找键或扫描所有存储的数据以删除 1 个值的情况。 他们仍然没有说明固定工作是否需要微秒或毫秒，因此延迟结果需要旁边的成功点和百分位。

留给以后的工作也需要限制，因此 WAL 文件具有最大大小，即使上传它是 O（文件字节）。 清理可能最终会检查或重写整个数据集，但每次运行都需要字节限制和保存的位置，以便在崩溃后可以恢复。 待处理队列还需要一个限制，因为写入创建旧字节的速度比清理删除旧字节的速度快，如果没有限制，廉价的请求路径只会隐藏一个不断增长的队列。

LLM 使写入上传程序、清理循环或复制日志的速度更快，而无需决定系统可能保留多少未完成的工作或何时必须减慢写入速度。 他们也无法选择何时可以安全返回成功、超时意味着什么，或者哪种崩溃可能会丢失数据。 这些决定仍然需要围绕 fdatasync() 进行记录和测试，使对象成为当前对象，更换写入器，并将写入内容复制到大多数服务器。

从内存写入本地 SSD、远程存储和副本之后，我可以更轻松地进行权衡。 更快的路径通常会在更少的工作之后停止，并且能够承受更少的故障，而稍后移动成功可以购买更多的耐用性，并且还可以使数据库负责协调、修复和清理。 只有将这些选项写在 GET、PUT 和 DELETE 数字旁边后，这些数字才变得有用。
